methodological_questions: identifying player gains in play types
controlling for confounding factors in role changes
defining player similarity (initiation profile, minutes, position)
identifying 'primary types' of an absent player

historical_evidence.finding: Similarity does not separate absorption from cascade; almost always findable. mean sim ABSORBED +0.863 vs CASCADE +0.848; Spearman(sim, -gap)=-0.19 (wrong-signed). Embiid 23-24 cascades with Reed sim 0.94.

The team-level BEST vs AVOID gap holds when H2 possessions are filtered to initiating player. Mean gap (n>=10 each tier) +0.427 PPP. Mean BEST 1.347 (38 players) vs AVOID 0.920 (94 players). Stars mean gap +0.542 (n=15) vs role +0.428 (n=16). Only 3 players clear n>=30 both tiers.
Shaper presence increases non-focal play-type diversity (entropy). d_entropy_nonfocal=-0.0455 (shaper, n_ts=80); organizer +0.0115. Paper interprets as 'rebalancing not expanding'; no CI given.

Connector absence displaces team offensive identity (D_A) more than usage-matched non-organizer absence. Unmatched conn vs role D_A 0.2020 vs 0.1021, t=5.97 p=2.87e-08. Usage-matched vs role: paired dD_A +0.1151, P(conn>ctrl)=81.2%, t=6.35 p=7.35e-09 n=96.
Teams and players differ in how often H2 trigger possessions land on the engine's BEST vs AVOID counter. Team AVOID% ranges 50.6% (ORL) to 6.8% (SAC); team BEST% 0.0%-15.8%.

Players score more on BEST-ranked counters than AVOID-ranked counters in the 55-series playsheets. 78 players with >=5 BEST and >=5 AVOID rows. Top gaps D. Lively II +1.833 (n=6/6), M. Brogdon +1.831 (7/11); some reverse (N. Jokic -0.333 n=8/18; L. Doncic -0.190 n=6/14). Stars mixed (D. White +0.864 n=49/42; SGA +0.33).

Named star initiators have identifiable lineup and forced-play-type suppressors in the possession graph. Jokic vs MIN lineup PPP 0.814, -0.385 (n=59); Curry vs HOU 0.851, -0.358 (n=47); Doncic vs LAC 0.733, -0.396 (n=30); Giannis forced PULL_UP 0.848, -0.540 vs preferred DRIVE (largest gap).

Routing possessions to each play type's best player adds value over A3, and survives defensive attention adaptation. V4 A5 vs A3 +0.77; V5 +0.94 (A5b vs A5 +0.01); V6 (520 matchups) A5 vs A3 +0.03, A5b vs A5 -0.00. Shrinks from +0.94 to +0.03 pts/100 on the larger 520-matchup sample.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Using player similarity to predict whether play types are absorbed or cascade when a player sits.
failed_approaches.why: B_powered_null (adequately powered null result); LIM:label_or_classification_error; RISK:LABEL_ERROR. Similarity did not separate absorption from cascade.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Detailed player-level analysis of BEST vs AVOID PPP gaps for initiators.
failed_approaches.why: LIM:small_sample; RISK:SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER. Only 3 players cleared n>=30 for both tiers, limiting generalizability.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Detecting an expansion of non-focal play-type diversity (entropy) with shaper presence.
failed_approaches.why: E_unclear (mechanism unclear from the records); d_entropy_nonfocal was near zero (-0.0455).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Hypothesis testing on player BEST/AVOID tier tendency.
failed_approaches.why: E_unclear (mechanism unclear from the records); no outcome test; small player samples (10-178 possessions).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Hypothesis testing on player-level BEST vs AVOID H2 PPP gaps.
failed_approaches.why: A_unanswerable (question not answerable with the data or design); RISK:PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE. n is small for most players (single-game playsheets); no multiplicity or clustered test.
E_unclear (mechanism unclear from the records); RISK:PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE. No placebo or matching; later sequence work treated similar star-chain gaps as artifacts.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Hypothesis that routing possessions to a play type's best player adds value and survives defensive attention.
failed_approaches.why: B_powered_null (adequately powered null result). The effect shrunk significantly on a larger sample, indicating null.

evidence_establishes: Player absence can significantly displace team offensive identity, and the type of player absent matters (FAM:SF-APPS-088).
Player-level initiation efficiency (PPP for BEST vs AVOID play types) can be measured, and meaningful differences exist (FAM:SF-APPS-036, FAM:SF-APPS-015, FAM:SF-APPA-048).
Offensive role changes due to player presence/absence tend to be 'rebalancing' of existing play types rather than expansion of repertoire (FAM:SF-PAP-008).
Simply having a 'similar-profile teammate' does not reliably predict how play types are reallocated (absorption vs. cascade) when a player is absent (FAM:SF-CHT-052).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether the 'closest pre-absence initiation profile' teammate (or most minutes/initiations/same-position minutes) is *the largest gainer* in the absent player's primary types.
A robust, generalizable method for defining and measuring 'player similarity' that predicts role reallocation outcomes.
A clear understanding of the mechanisms behind observed shifts in play-type distribution after player absence.
How to reliably identify 'primary types' of an absent player that are then reallocated.
own_inferences: The concept of 'player similarity' is complex and likely needs to go beyond simple initiation profile overlap to predict reallocation outcomes effectively, given that a simple similarity measure was found to be inconclusive (FAM:SF-CHT-052).

The 'largest gainer' metric needs careful definition (e.g., absolute volume, percentage increase, efficiency improvement) and will likely suffer from small sample sizes at the player-absence event level.

The unit of analysis (absence spells, n=148, 11 cases) suggests a very limited number of distinct player absences for robust statistical inference, especially when trying to compare specific teammates.

The question implies a causal link, which will require careful control for confounders beyond just player similarity, such as opponent, game context, and other roster changes during the absence period.
uncertainties: The precise definition of 'closest pre-absence initiation profile' remains open. Is it based on volume, efficiency, specific play types, or a composite score?
How 'primary types' of the absent player will be identified and quantified.
How 'largest gainer' will be measured (e.g., raw volume increase, percentage increase, increase in efficiency, share of team's increase).
The exact methodology for comparing pre- and post-absence periods, including duration and baseline adjustment.
The representativeness and statistical power of the '11 cases' mentioned in the data description for robust inference on player-level effects.

historical_effect.explanation: The historical evidence, particularly FAM:SF-CHT-052, strongly suggests that a straightforward definition of 'similarity' is unlikely to be a robust predictor of how roles are reallocated. This significantly lowers the predicted probability of supporting the hypothesis as stated. Furthermore, repeated findings of 'small sample size' (FAM:SF-APPS-036, FAM:SF-APPS-088, FAM:SF-APPA-048) for player-level analyses underscore the challenge of the current sample size (11 cases), moving the decision from 'proceed' to 'do_not_proceed' without substantial changes, or at least a 'proceed_with_changes' if the scope is narrowed significantly.

blocking_constraints.text: The stated units (n=148 spells, 11 cases) are extremely small for a player-level hypothesis that involves identifying 'the largest gainer' among multiple teammates for specific play types. This will lead to very low statistical power and high uncertainty in findings, mirroring limitations seen in FAM:SF-APPS-036 and FAM:SF-APPA-048.

Changes in teammate roles can be confounded by various factors beyond the absent player's profile and the closest teammate's profile, including opponent, game situations, coach's strategy, other simultaneous roster changes, and the performance of other teammates. The current question doesn't specify controls for these.

Defining 'closest pre-absence initiation profile' and 'largest gainer in the absent player's primary types' requires robust, reliable metrics. The historical evidence (FAM:SF-CHT-052) suggests that simple similarity metrics might not be reliable predictors of reallocation outcomes. The definition of 'primary types' and 'gains' must be carefully considered to avoid arbitrary labels or measurement error.

prior_work.summary: Previous work confirms that player absence leads to offensive identity displacement (FAM:SF-APPS-088) and that offensive reorganization involves rebalancing existing play types rather than expanding repertoire (FAM:SF-PAP-008). However, a direct test of 'similarity' predicting reallocation patterns was inconclusive (FAM:SF-CHT-052), suggesting the core premise of the current question might be overly simplistic or require a more nuanced definition of similarity and reallocation. Player-level efficiency metrics for play types have been developed but suffer from small sample sizes for robust hypothesis testing (FAM:SF-APPS-036, FAM:SF-APPA-048).

risks.text: With only 11 'cases' (likely unique player absences) and 148 'spells' (individual games within absences), identifying 'the largest gainer' among potentially multiple teammates for specific play types will lead to extremely sparse data for each comparison, severely limiting statistical power and the ability to detect true effects or generalize findings.

Role changes are influenced by many factors (e.g., opponent, game flow, other injuries, coaching decisions, other teammates' performance). Without proper controls, attributing gains solely to the absent player's profile and the 'closest' teammate's profile is highly susceptible to confounding bias.

The operational definitions of 'closest pre-absence initiation profile,' 'absent player's primary types,' and 'largest gainer' are critical. If these measures are not robust or are susceptible to noise, the conclusions will be unreliable. The finding from FAM:SF-CHT-052 on similarity not separating absorption from cascade highlights this risk.

Identifying 'the largest gainer' could be sensitive to the chosen metric (e.g., raw volume, percentage share, efficiency gain) and period of measurement, potentially leading to an outcome-derived label that is not robust.
Some play types might have inherently low base rates of initiation, making 'gains' in those types statistically volatile and hard to interpret.

design.estimand: The average difference in the change in primary play-type initiation volume (or share) for the most similar teammate compared to other teammates following a key player's absence.
design.unit: Player-absence event (a single player's absence from a contiguous set of games).
design.sample: NBA 2022-23 to 2025-26 seasons, focusing on 'key player' absences (e.g., top-3 usage or minutes per team). A 'case' is a unique player absence. A 'spell' is a game within an absence. Given n=11 cases, this sample is insufficient for robust testing of the detailed hypothesis.
design.power: Not achievable with the current sample size for a player-level hypothesis. A minimum of 50-100 player-absence events would likely be required to achieve even modest power for detecting a medium effect size for 'largest gainer' comparisons, assuming multiple teammates per absence.
design.controls: Control for game-level confounders (opponent strength, game score, pace) using fixed effects or regression adjustments. Control for other simultaneous player absences/returns. Use a difference-in-differences approach comparing teammate play-type initiations pre- and post-absence, relative to a baseline or control group (e.g., other teammates, or similar teams without key absences).
design.falsification: The hypothesis would be falsified if the teammate with the closest profile (or most minutes/initiations/same-position minutes) does not show a statistically significant 'largest gain' in the absent player's primary play types compared to other teammates, or if other teammates consistently show larger gains.
design.multiplicity: Given the small sample, avoid multiple comparisons of different similarity metrics or 'gainer' definitions. Pre-specify one primary similarity metric and one primary 'gainer' metric. If multiple primary types are analyzed, apply a Bonferroni correction or similar adjustment for multiple hypothesis testing.
design.decision_rule: Reject the null hypothesis (that similarity does not predict largest gainer) if the p-value for the primary estimand is less than 0.05, and the effect size is practically meaningful (e.g., >X % increase in initiation share for the similar player). Given the low power, this rule is unlikely to lead to a supported finding.
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26 seasons, using derived play-type possession records from the NBA stats API, including initiator, play type, and points. Player similarity profiles derived from pre-absence play-type initiation volumes/efficiencies.

methodological_questions: identifying player gains in play types
controlling for confounding factors in role changes
